find: Violence intensified in 1190. As crusading fever swept England before the Third Crusade, anti-Jewish riots broke out in London and several other cities.
replace: Violence intensified in 1189 and 1190. As crusading fever swept England before the Third Crusade, a massacre of Jews took place in London at Richard I’s coronation in September 1189, and riots followed in 1190 at King’s Lynn, Norwich, Stamford, Lincoln and Bury St Edmunds.
note: F20: the London massacre was at Richard I's coronation on 3 September 1189, not 1190.

find: The blood libel accusations were repeatedly investigated and debunked by the authorities — Henry III at one point imprisoned the accusers of a Jewish community rather than the Jews themselves.
replace: The blood libel was not believed everywhere — Pope Innocent IV condemned the accusation as false in 1247.
note: F21: the Henry III claim is unsupported and runs against his record; after the death of Hugh of Lincoln in 1255 he had about 18 Jews hanged.

find: While Whig politicians like Lord Godolphin initially welcomed them as Protestant brethren, the sheer scale of arrivals strained charitable resources and generated hostility.

note: F22: Godolphin was a Tory by background leading a Whig-dependent ministry; the 1709 general naturalisation act was the Whig measure that drew the Palatines.

find: On 22 June 1948, the Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury, Essex, carrying 492 passengers from the Caribbean — most of them from Jamaica. They had legal right to be there: the British Nationality Act, passed just weeks earlier, confirmed that all Commonwealth subjects were British citizens.
replace: On 22 June 1948, passengers came ashore from the Empire Windrush at Tilbury, Essex. The ship’s passenger list records 1,027 people, and 802 of them gave a Caribbean country as their last home; most were Jamaican. The figure of 492 that is often quoted came from press reports that counted only some of the men on board. They had a legal right to be there: they were born in British colonies, so they were already British subjects, and the British Nationality Act passed later in 1948 confirmed that Commonwealth citizens could come to Britain.
note: F10/F11: the 1948 Act got royal assent on 30 July 1948, after the ship docked, and came into force on 1 January 1949; the manifest records 1,027 passengers, 802 of them from the Caribbean.
